en: The Chinese people trudged along.
The Black Kalmyks, the many Manchus,
Unable to endure the fury
Of that fierce Kalcha,
Floundered ahead of him.
It-Ölbös, where they fought—
It was a journey of forty days;
All the heroes favored by Kydyr
Would perish in that place.
There was no mountain the size of a knucklebone,
No hollow the size of a saddlecloth.
When a swan flew there, its ears
Burned in that desert.
There was no grass to pinch and eat,
No water to make a drop of broth.
A hero traveling there would find no livestock;
It was a desert of forty days.
All the mighty ones,
It was time for them to face one another.
Then, with golden forelock and tasseled sash,
Azizkan’s Almambet,
Your champion, ahead of an arrow,
Reached brave Mangküsh.
Their champion, giant Mangküsh,
Your Almambet, as soon as he reached him,
From atop his rhinoceros
Knocked flat and swept past.
Before a san of swift foot-runners
Could swarm up together,
Their champion, giant Mangküsh,
Before they could carry him to safety,
The companion of his very life,
I do not know whence he came,
Khan Baltay’s Chubak.
Tall in body, broad in shoulders,
The edge of black steel,
Have you heard of him,
Khan Baltay’s Chubak?
He herded white deer and made them cattle;
When his anger was aroused,
He threw all men into turmoil.
No man had strength to wrestle him;
He never relaxed his grimness,
Never drew back from a thrust,
Never retreated at the sight of an enemy.
Taking the sword Oykuma in hand,
Chubak reached him then.
As soon as he reached Mangküsh,
Making his blood fall like hail,
He struck off his head and swept past.
When their dear Mangküsh died,
When the Manchus met with grief,
Then Kongurbay, khan of the shaven ones,
His roar splitting stone,
His saddle-flaps fluttering,
The forelock at his nape
Waving like a mallet,
His eyes like the bed of a lake,
Grew angry and shouted,
Alöökö’s Kongurbay.
The space between his brows
Was like an exposed bed of embers.
His tread raised dust;
His voice drove out men’s souls.
Making the steed Algara strain,
Jerking the golden lead-rope,
Making the earth split and rumble,
Alöökö’s Kongurbay
Came thundering.
His golden-cheeked battle-axe
He looped over his wrist.
The double-edged Zulpukor
He drew from its sheath.
Wind came from his mouth;
Fire poured from his eyes.
The lacquered lance he gripped
Cracked as though it would break.
His great teeth, broad as doors,
Crumbled like millet.
Breaking out at Chubak’s flank,
Looming like a huge mountain,
Burning with rage and distress,
To reach brave Chubak,
Kongurbay drew near.
If he reached Chubak,
From atop Kögala
He would knock him flat and sweep past.
When Kongurbay came close to Chubak,
The Chinese of forty tribes grew frenzied.
All the swift foot-runners
Joined in a frenzy to reach Chubak.
Without entering the very center of the fight,
Had he not been keeping to the edge,
Your Almambet, born under a lucky star?
“How fares noble Chubak?”
Had your Almambet not been watching?
“If my death comes, I shall die;
While I am alive, beside Chubak
I shall stand,” he said.
Not letting him reach your Chubak,
Kalcha, khan of the shaven ones,
Your Almambet reached with a mighty stretch.
As soon as he reached Kalcha,
From atop Algara,
Your Almambet knocked him flat and swept past.
(What you see today is gone tomorrow;
Heroes, such is this unruly world.
The Chinese are in ilek; he is alone.
What has the world not done?)
His feet dangled loose;
From atop Algara
Kongurbay toppled.
The massed Chinese, the many Manchus,
Their dear fierce Kalcha
Surrounded then.
Occupied with Kalcha,
All the Chinese of forty tribes remained.
A champion named Eybe,
A champion named Sheybe,
Arrived ahead of an arrow.
Reaching him, they set him on his horse;
Their accomplished Kalcha
They carried away without letting him die.
He sent word to his khan,
Sent a letter saying, “Give me troops,”
To the lower city of the kakan.
The earth turned to dust;
Seventy Beijings rose in motion.
People upon people came.
When the Chinese swept over them,
The earth shook and swayed.
Then they were drenched in bloody blood;
The heroes stood and fought without fleeing.
They took no rest by day;
At night they did not sleep.
The heroes who entered the holy war,
Even if they died, had no regrets.
Then wounded Kongurbay,
Kongurbay in a wretched state,
When struck, two of his ribs
Had been shattered.
Alöökö’s Kongurbay
Coughed in sharp bursts
And raised his head like a deer.
When he cried out, from his mouth
Blood came in gushes.
Unable to match them in battle,
Kongurbay’s strength ebbed.
Coughing again and again,
Your champion raised his neck like a stag.
When he rumbled, from his mouth
Dark blood came by the shovelful.
Alöökö’s Kongurbay
Was left sorely helpless.
Kongurbay was wounded,
Suffering a great deal.
Sending word to his khan,
He dispatched a letter
To that nearby city of the kakan.
Forty thousand skilled practitioners
Made themselves ready.
From whatever remedies there were,
They managed to rub some on him.
When his skilled practitioners came,
“Allow a term of seven days,” they said,
And asked for a respite.
His marksmen who never missed
Gathered afresh;
The Chinese came swarming.
Those who fired in the night,
The various unbelievers, formed separate bands.
Clad in mottled green,
Their marksmen came into view.
Along Kum-Kyya’s road at the edge,
They came swarming then.
You could not tell whether they were worms;
They came seething then.
Kongurbay, khan of the shaven ones,
Had recovered from his illness.
Setting them before him and beating them,
He was driving them on then.
Unable to endure his fury,
The massed Chinese, a san of Manchus,
Thronging like ants,
Had spread everywhere then.
They were a Chinese people of forty tribes,
With lion Kalcha in their midst.
The eighteen thousand worlds
They were about to trample.
At a ridge curved like a saddle-pass,
He turned Sarala’s head.
With golden forelock and tasseled sash,
Azizkan’s only son,
In his grief, to Chubak
Now spoke his final wishes:
“Turn your horse’s head a moment;
Lucky when you go out to a shooting fight,
My precious Chubak, stand a moment!
A deep-dug pit is coming;
Look, a black day weighs heavily upon life!
Clad in mottled blue iron,
Their fierce warrior is coming out.
Able to thrust a lance without looking,
Their mighty man is coming out.
Kozhozhash and Kongurbay,
Able to fight with lances without stirring,
Their mighty men are coming out.
Thick as the hairs on a cow,
Your Chinese have swarmed over everything!
A deep-dug pit is coming;
Seething misfortune is coming;
A black day weighs heavily upon life.
What an age, what a day,
Hero, what sort of day will it be!
The massed Chinese have risen;
Ah, hero, will they surround us?
To rescue you,
Your lion, generous Manas, is absent.
Ah, hero, will your death come thus?
With their great Kalcha at their head,
Ah, hero, will they gather and seize us?
Together tormenting this life,
Ah, hero, will they slaughter us as a sacrifice?
Before the khan of Chin,
‘Here is the head of the true enemy!’
Ah, hero, will they take it as glad tidings?
If the Chinese kill me today,
Will these bones remain unburied?
My dear eyes, like a young camel’s,
Will cawing crows peck them out?
This flesh, pure and fair,
Will white vultures tear and feast on it?
Will wolves dig out the kidneys?
My great teeth, broad as doors,
Will magpies shit on them?
On the hills are white-headed horses;
When one dies exchanging shots,
Where might this wretched head not lie!
What God has written,
There is no way not to bear it.
If we depart from this world,
To remain and give support,
There is no male child behind us!
If we die out of this world,
There is no ear to hear:
‘My poor father has died!’
To recite the Quran,
There is no male heir behind us!
My Chubak, we shall not withdraw to Talas alive;
We shall not return from Beijing alive.
If I die at Chinese hands,
If you survive me,
Take me by the waist and fold me over.
My hero Chubak, my blood-friend,
Load my bones for Mecca!
If you come upon a place with a shrine,
